module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Is Every Convex Polyhedron Rupert?

A polyhedron is Rupert if one can cut a hole in it and pass another
copy of the same polyhedron through that hole.

More formally: a convex body in ℝ³ is a compact, convex set with
nonempty interior. A convex body X is said to be Rupert if there are
two affine transforms T₁, T₂ ∈ SE(3) such that π(T₁(X)) ⊆
int(π(T₂(X))), where π : ℝ³ → ℝ² is the evident projection, and int
denotes topological interior.

Not all convex bodies are Rupert. For example,
- the unit ball is not Rupert
- the circular cylinder of unit diameter and height
  closed on each end by disks is not Rupert

However, many convex polyhedra are Rupert. All Platonic solids, and
most Archimedean and Catalan solids are known to be Rupert.

Question: are all convex polyhedra with nonempty interior Rupert?

*References:*

* [Platonic Passages](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/314715434_Platonic_Passages),
  R. P. Jerrard, J. E. Wetzel, and L. Yuan., Math. Mag., 90(2):87–98,
  2017. conjectures ("with a certain hesitancy") that perhaps all
  convex polyhedra are Rupert.

* However, [An Algorithmic Approach to Rupert's Problem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.13754#cite.JeWeYu17)
  describes experimental evidence to suggest that three Archimedean
  solids may not be Rupert.

* [Optimizing for the Rupert property](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00601)
  is the source of some of the Catalan solid results, and has more
  results for Johnson polyhedra as well.

* [This video by David Renshaw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=evKFok65t_E) visualizes
  known results for Platonic, Archimedean, and Catalan solids.

* This problem's name comes from the fact that it is a generalization
  of [Prince Rupert's Cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Rupert%27s_cube).

* [A convex polyhedron without Rupert's property](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18475),
  Jakob Steininger and Sergey Yurkevich, 2025. Constructs a convex polyhedron and
  a proof that it is not Rupert, resolving the open question.

-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Rupert

open scoped Matrix

abbrev SO3 := Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup (Fin 3) ℝ

scoped notation "ℝ²" => Fin 2 → ℝ
scoped notation "ℝ³" => Fin 3 → ℝ

/--
The result of transforming a subset of ℝ³ by a chosen rotation and offset,
and then projected to ℝ².
-/
def transformed_shadow (X : Set ℝ³) (offset : ℝ²) (rotation : SO3) : Set ℝ² :=
  (fun p ↦ offset + (rotation *ᵥ p) ∘ Fin.castSucc) '' X

/--
A convex polyhedron (given as a finite collection of vertices) is Rupert if
there are two rotations in ℝ³ (called "inner" and "outer") and a translation in ℝ²
such that the "inner shadow" (the projection to ℝ² of the inner rotation applied
to the polyhedron, then translated) fits in the interior of the "outer shadow"
(the projection to ℝ² of the outer rotation applied to the polyhedron)

[Note: The restriction to (polyhedra determined by the convex hulls of)
*finite* sets of vertices here is deliberate. Were we to generalize to
arbitrary subsets of ℝⁿ we'd probably want to make the containment
relation more strict, e.g.
  closure inner_shadow ⊆ interior outer_shadow
to rule out, e.g. the open ball being Rupert. However, we didn't
observe any such generalization in the literature yet, so we stuck to
what was in the citations above.]
-/
def IsRupert (vertices : Finset ℝ³) : Prop :=
   ∃ (inner_rotation : SO3) (inner_offset : ℝ²) (outer_rotation : SO3),
   let inner_shadow := transformed_shadow (convexHull ℝ vertices) inner_offset inner_rotation
   let outer_shadow := transformed_shadow (convexHull ℝ vertices) 0 outer_rotation
   inner_shadow ⊆ interior outer_shadow

/--
There exists a convex polyhedron with nonempty interior for which the Rupert property does
not hold.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/jcreedcmu/Noperthedron/blob/1ee88118097acc9db768b44b3c6ea9f60a4e4b67/KernelCaseAnalysis/ProofOfMainTheorem.lean#L21"]
theorem is_every_convex_polyhedron_rupert :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ (vertices : Finset ℝ³),
       (interior (convexHull ℝ vertices : Set ℝ³)).Nonempty → IsRupert vertices := by
 sorry

reformulations.difference: The Lean definition uses two rotations R₁, R₂ ∈ SO(3), then the coordinate projection (x,y,z) ↦ (x,y), plus a translation applied only to the inner shadow. It asks that the image of the convex hull fit in the interior of the other image. The sources state it differently. Steininger–Yurkevich 2021 (arXiv 2112.13754, Prop. 1) use parametrized orthogonal projections M(θ,φ), a planar rotation R(α) and a translation T_{x,y}, applied to the vertex set, with containment in the interior of the convex hull of the projected vertices. For point-symmetric polyhedra, SY 2025 (Def. 2) drop the translation. The module docstring uses two rigid motions T₁, T₂ ∈ SE(3).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (a) The maps {π∘R : R ∈ SO(3)} are exactly the 2×3 matrices with orthonormal rows. So are the maps {R(α)M(θ,φ)}. The rows of M(θ,φ) are orthonormal with cross product X(θ,φ). Any orthonormal pair (u,v) extends to (u; v; u×v) ∈ SO(3). Two positively oriented orthonormal frames of the same plane differ by a planar rotation. (b) A rotation or translation on the outer side can be moved to the inner side, because the interior commutes with planar isometries. 3D translations project to planar translations, so SE(3) × SE(3) reduces to SO(3) × SO(3) plus one planar offset. (c) Reflections add nothing: π∘diag(1,1,−1) = π. (d) π∘R is linear, so it maps convex hulls to convex hulls. The interior of a convex set is convex. So the projected hull lies in the interior iff the projected vertices do. (e) The topology on `Fin 2 → ℝ` is the product topology, i.e. the Euclidean one. I checked this with `rfl`.

reformulations.difference: The theorem quantifies over every `Finset (Fin 3 → ℝ)` whose convex hull has nonempty interior. The sources quantify over 'convex polyhedra': SY define a polyhedron as a finite non-degenerate set of points in ℝ³ in convex position. The settled answer appears as `answer(False) ↔ ∀ ...`, i.e. 'some polyhedron is not Rupert'.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `IsRupert` depends only on `convexHull ℝ vertices`. The convex hull of a finite set equals the convex hull of its extreme points, and those are in convex position. In ℝ³ such a hull is non-degenerate exactly when it has nonempty interior. So both universal statements range over the same convex bodies. `False ↔ P` is `¬P`, i.e. 'there is a non-Rupert polyhedron', which is SY 2025's Theorem 1.

review.notes:
I found no misformalization and no stale status. The file is marked `research solved` with `answer(False)` and a `formal_proof` link. This matches Steininger–Yurkevich 2025 (arXiv 2508.18475): their Noperthedron is not Rupert, which disproves the 2017 conjecture.

Checks run in /workspace/review:
- `#print` of the definitions. The topologies on `Fin 2 → ℝ` and `Fin 3 → ℝ` are `Pi.topologicalSpace` (checked with `rfl`).
- The shadow parses as `offset + ((R *ᵥ p) ∘ Fin.castSucc)`, i.e. the projection onto coordinates 0 and 1.
- `SO3` membership means orthogonal with determinant 1, using the trivial star on ℝ.

`formal_proof` check, following PROOFS.md: the link points to `Noperthedron.KernelCaseAnalysis.exists_not_rupert : ExistsNonRupertPolyhedron`. The linked `IsRupert` and `ExistsNonRupertPolyhedron` are stated on `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)` and `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`. I copied these definitions from Noperthedron/MainTheorem.lean at the linked commit into /workspace/review/equiv.lean. There I proved, with no `sorry` (`#print axioms`: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound), that the file's statement `(False ↔ ∀ vertices, ... → Rupert.IsRupert vertices)` is equivalent to `ExistsNonRupertPolyhedron`. So the linked theorem implies the repository statement. I did not build the external project; its README says the kernel check takes about 50 core-hours. The file's own `#print axioms` comment lists only the three standard axioms.

Docstring remarks (not findings):
1. The module docstring says 2112.13754 'describes experimental evidence to suggest that three Archimedean solids may not be Rupert'. The paper's algorithm failed on three Archimedean solids (rhombicosidodecahedron, snub cube, snub dodecahedron). But it conjectures non-Rupertness, from statistical evidence, only for the rhombicosidodecahedron. For the two snubs it says 'we did not estimate the Rupertness and hence have no statistical evidence' and that more computation might find solutions. The authors were initially 'quite skeptical' that the snubs are Rupert. So the paraphrase is loose but defensible; the maintainers might tighten it.
2. The claim that the cylinder of unit diameter and unit height is not Rupert is correct. When height ≥ diameter, every projection has minimum width exactly equal to the diameter, so no projection fits strictly inside another.
3. I could not read the 'with a certain hesitancy' quote from Jerrard–Wetzel–Yuan (paywalled). SY 2021/2025 and Wikipedia agree that this 2017 paper posed or suggested the conjecture.
